name: Post-Hardcore
about: Post-hardcore began around 1985 when American hardcore bands slowed down and let dissonance, dynamics and melody back in. Washington's Revolution Summer produced Rites of Spring and Embrace, and from their ashes Ian MacKaye and Guy Picciotto formed Fugazi, whose dub-tinged, tightly disciplined records on Dischord are the genre's center. Chicago's Big Black and Steve Albini, San Diego's Drive Like Jehu, Olympia's Unwound and D.C.'s Jawbox pushed the guitars toward angular noise and odd lengths, while Quicksand kept the heaviness. The sound is tense rather than fast: interlocking guitars, a strong rhythm section and voices that move between speech, song and scream. At the Drive-In and Refused made it briefly commercial around 2000, and Touché Amoré and La Dispute carried its confessional side into the 2010s.

artists.name: Fugazi
artists.why: the genre's center and its conscience

artists.name: Hüsker Dü
artists.why: first to slow hardcore into something bigger

artists.name: At the Drive-In
artists.why: El Paso chaos that briefly went mainstream

albums.title: New Day Rising
albums.why: Bob Mould and Grant Hart's pop songs buried under hardcore speed and white noise, with Celebrated Summer the moment the genre learned to be wistful.

albums.title: Rites of Spring
albums.why: Guy Picciotto's cracked, pleading voice over hardcore that kept stopping to feel something: the record that invented emo and refused the name.

albums.title: Atomizer
albums.why: Steve Albini's drum machine, two treble-heavy guitars and songs about arson and small-town boredom, as cold and precise as the sound it influenced.

albums.title: Embrace
albums.why: Ian MacKaye's short-lived band between Minor Threat and Fugazi sang, rather than shouted, about self-doubt, and the Revolution Summer had its second pillar.

albums.title: 13 Songs
albums.why: The first two EPs on one disc, with Waiting Room's dub bass line and Picciotto's Glue Man, is the most-played introduction to the genre and still its best.

albums.title: Repeater
albums.why: Ian MacKaye and Guy Picciotto's first full album turned dub, dissonance and discipline into post-hardcore's defining statement.

albums.title: Goat
albums.why: David Yow's drunken ravings over Duane Denison's surgical guitar and Albini's room sound made the noisiest great rock record of the early 1990s.

albums.title: 13-Point Program to Destroy America
albums.why: Ian Svenonius's mock-revolutionary manifesto with free-jazz trumpet and garage chaos, the D.C. scene's funniest and most stylish record.

albums.title: Slip
albums.why: Walter Schreifels left youth crew for down-tuned, groove-heavy songs like Dine Alone and Fazer, the New York model for 1990s post-hardcore.

albums.title: Venus Luxure No. 1 Baby
albums.why: Two basses, Scott McCloud's lounge-lizard mutter and Ted Niceley's production made D.C. post-hardcore sound sleazy and danceable for the first time.

albums.title: For Your Own Special Sweetheart
albums.why: J. Robbins's band took Dischord's angularity to Atlantic and made it bigger without blunting it, and Savory remains the D.C. sound's best single.

albums.title: Yank Crime
albums.why: Rick Froberg's shriek over John Reis's serrated guitar across nine-minute songs made a dense, difficult major-label record that became a cult scripture.

albums.title: At Action Park
albums.why: Albini, Bob Weston and Todd Trainer's debut is minimal, aluminum-necked and dry, every note placed with the care of the engineer behind it.

albums.title: Pony Express Record
albums.why: Craig Wedren's operatic falsetto and the band's lurching, glam-tinged structures made the strangest post-hardcore record a major label ever released.

albums.title: Repetition
albums.why: Justin Trosper's trio hit their stride on an album of taut, dissonant tension with Corpse Pose as its anchor, Olympia's answer to Fugazi.

albums.title: The Shape of Punk to Come
albums.why: The Swedish band's farewell mixed hardcore, jazz, techno and manifesto, and its influence on 2000s heavy music outstripped its initial reception.

albums.title: Relationship of Command
albums.why: Ross Robinson's production and One Armed Scissor put Cedric Bixler-Zavala's surreal howl on television, and the band split at the moment of arrival.

albums.title: Full Collapse
albums.why: Geoff Rickly's New Brunswick band brought post-hardcore's scream-and-sing dynamic to a generation, with Understanding in a Car Crash the breakthrough.

albums.title: Leaves Turn Inside You
albums.why: A double album of Mellotrons, drones and slow-building songs, the band's farewell is its masterpiece and the genre's most patient record.

albums.title: Suicide Invoice
albums.why: Reis and Froberg's post-Jehu band stripped the epics down to two-minute garage-punk sprints with the same serrated guitars and spleen.

albums.title: Worship and Tribute
albums.why: Daryl Palumbo's range and the band's Long Island mix of hardcore, soul and metal produced the most musically ambitious record of the 2002 scene.

albums.title: Brother, Sister
albums.why: Aaron Weiss's spoken-word parables about spiders, faith and failure over spidery post-hardcore guitars, a Philadelphia record with no real precedent.

albums.title: Wildlife
albums.why: Jordan Dreyer's short stories of grief and violence, half spoken and half screamed over Grand Rapids guitars, made the 2010s' most literary post-hardcore album.

albums.title: Stage Four
albums.why: Jeremy Bolm's account of his mother's death, sung as much as screamed over the Los Angeles band's brightest arrangements, is the genre's modern grief record.
